paragraphs: A towed field gun hidden under a camouflage net, the classic concealed artillery position for military and war scenes. The Tactical Net with Towed Cannon uses 292,326 polygons, much of it in the knotted netting draped over the barrel.

Its 297,209 vertices let the net sag over the barrel and carriage while the gun shield and wheels stay sharply defined. Built to CheckMate standards, the emplacement arrives with clean geometry and realistic artillery proportions. The netting breaks up the outline of the cannon, which is exactly how crews hide positions from aerial observation.

At $179 since 2026, the position suits war films, strategy games and military history documentaries. Dig it into a tree line beside ammunition crates, or place it in a field trench under overcast skies. Military museums and reenactment groups can show how artillery was concealed without staging a full deployment. Swapping the net color in your renderer adapts the position to desert, forest or winter terrain.

A set of Vivid Scribbles dot grid journals with illustrated covers, ready for planners, bullet journal fans and stationery shelves. The Vivid Scribbles Dot Grid Journal Set brings 22,674 polygons across several notebooks, each with a rounded spine and page block.

There are 23,073 vertices, enough for soft cover corners and a visible stack of pages along each edge. Thanks to StemCell rules the journals arrive in a variety of native formats tied to one master scene. Bright cover artwork contrasts with the clean dot grid inside, giving the books a cheerful, creative personality.

This 2026 journal set costs $29 and suits student desks, home office renders and craft room interiors. Fan them out beside washi tape and colored pens, or stack them neatly on a bookshelf. Stationery shops can stage a seasonal display of journals without photographing physical samples. Each journal is a separate object, so one can sit open while the others stay closed.

A Vivid Scribbles journal with a sunflower cover and dotted pages, a bright companion for daily planning and creative notes. This single notebook needs 7,558 polygons for its cover, page edges and gently rounded spine.

With 7,691 vertices, the cover corners stay soft and the page stack reads as layered paper. StemCell output gives the journal several native formats, all exported from a common master scene. The golden sunflower artwork draws the eye, making the notebook a strong focal point on a plain desk.

Two versions are available at $19 each: the Vivid Scribbles Dot Journal and the Vivid Scribbles Lavender Dot Grid Journal. The lavender edition offers a cooler, calmer palette, while the sunflower cover feels warm and sunny. Both came out in 2026 and suit planner flat lays, study scenes and cozy reading nooks. Lay one open with a pen across the pages, as if a to-do list is halfway written.

A compact vlogging camera mounted on a battery grip handle, the handheld rig creators use to film themselves on the move. The Vlogging Camera with Battery Handle carries 27,908 polygons for the lens, flip screen, buttons and textured grip.

Its 28,746 vertices keep the lens barrel round and the grip contours comfortable looking in close shots. Being StemCell certified, the camera arrives in a full range of native formats from a single checked scene. The battery handle extends the grip below the body, giving a character something natural to hold at arm's length.

Released in 2026 at $44, the rig suits influencer scenes, travel vlogs and content creator animations. Put it in a traveler's hand on a busy street, or rest it beside a laptop in a home studio. Camera retailers can show the grip and body together, which helps buyers picture a complete setup. A front-facing screen lets the creator frame their own face, a key detail for any vlogging scene.

A mounted water cannon with twin control handles, the nozzle used by firefighters and riot control vehicles to direct heavy streams. The Water Cannon with Control Handles is lean at 5,738 polygons, covering the barrel, swivel joint and grips.

There are 5,867 vertices, enough for a smooth nozzle and a believable rotating base. Built under CheckMate requirements, the cannon opens with clean geometry at the size of real equipment. The paired handles let an operator aim with both hands, a detail that sells the weight of the jet.

This 2026 cannon is priced at $29 and suits fire station scenes, industrial safety films and vehicle builds. Mount it on the roof of a fire truck, a fireboat deck or the edge of a refinery tank farm. Low geometry means it can sit on distant vehicles without adding noticeable weight to the scene. Add a particle stream from the nozzle and the static prop becomes an action shot.

A glass snow globe holding a decorated Christmas tree, a festive keepsake for holiday interiors and seasonal greeting scenes. The Winter Snow Globe with Festive Tree uses 1,260,585 polygons, capturing ornaments, needles and the flakes suspended inside.

Its 4,792,773 vertices make this a heavy hero piece, with fine detail meant for macro photography and slow close-ups. Approved under CheckMate standards, the globe arrives with clean, separable parts for glass, base and scene. The clear dome magnifies the tree slightly, and refraction in your renderer will make the scene inside sparkle.

From 2026 the globe has been offered at $39 for holiday product shots, festive animations and winter interiors. Set it on a mantel beside candles, or shake it in an animation to send snow swirling around the tree. Gift shops preparing seasonal catalogs can show it without photographing fragile glass in a studio. For wide room shots, a lighter stand-in will save memory while this version takes the close-ups.

A snow globe enclosing a little gingerbread house with icing trim, a sweet decoration for Christmas mantels and holiday windows. The Winter Snow Globe with Gingerbread House uses 87,069 polygons, giving the cookie walls, candy details and base clean shape.

There are 86,180 vertices, a balanced count that keeps the dome round and the roof edges crisp. Its CheckMate certification means organized parts, so the glass dome can be hidden or replaced easily. The tiny house sits on a snowy mound, and its warm colors glow against the cold glass.

The globe went into the catalog in 2026 at $39 and fits seasonal greeting scenes, toy shops and cozy interiors. Place it on a windowsill with frost on the panes, or wrap it in a gift box under the tree. Compared with the tree version, this lighter build suits wider shots where several decorations share the frame. Bakeries and confectioners can echo their own gingerbread products in festive window designs.

A PlayStation 5 console in a Wolverine-themed finish with its DualSense controller, ready for gaming rooms and living room setups. The Wolverine PS5 with DualSense uses 47,264 polygons for the console shell, stand and controller buttons.

Its 51,082 vertices keep the curved side panels and controller grips smooth in close shots. Made to CheckMate requirements, the console and controller arrive as separate, correctly scaled objects. The themed panels set it apart from the standard white console at a glance.

Available since 2026 for $59, the console fits gamer bedrooms, esports lounges and tech review scenes. Stand it beside a television on a media unit, or leave the controller on a sofa cushion mid-session. Collectors' rooms gain a special edition piece that stands out among regular consoles on the shelf. The vertical stand keeps the slim console upright, matching how most owners display it next to a screen.

A female figure wearing a delicate white lace eye mask, an elegant subject for masquerade, fashion and portrait scenes. The Woman with Lace Eye Mask White uses 58,461 polygons, shaping the face, hair and openwork lace around the eyes.

There are 79,644 vertices, with extra density in the lace cutouts that frame the eyes. The model follows CheckMate requirements, arriving with a clean structure and human proportions. White lace against skin creates a soft contrast that reads as mysterious rather than theatrical.

Available in 2026 at $69, the figure suits beauty visuals, masquerade ball scenes and fashion editorials. Pose the figure at a candlelit gala, or place it in a studio portrait with a dark backdrop. Book cover designers working on romance or mystery titles can build a striking image around the mask. Soft side lighting picks out the lace pattern and gives the face a gentle, cinematic glow.

A traditional wooden broom with a long handle and bundled bristles, a humble tool for barns, cottages and witch stories. The Wooden Broom spends 472,088 polygons on individual straw strands, so the head looks full and slightly frayed.

Its 485,228 vertices allow each bristle to bend on its own rather than forming a solid block. CheckMate certification confirms clean geometry and a handle length that matches a real broom. Cord binding wraps the bristles tightly at the top, the detail that marks a handmade broom.

The broom became available in 2026 at $29 and suits rustic interiors, farm scenes and Halloween settings. Lean it against a barn door beside a pile of hay, or send a witch flying across a full moon on it. For crowded scenes, consider a lighter broom, since this version is built for close inspection. Folk museums and craft studios can show traditional broom making through close views of the binding.

A crude wooden warning sign nailed to a post, marking a minefield in war zones, borderlands and abandoned battlefields. The Wooden Mine Warning Sign with Post Game Ready is remarkably light, built from just 37 polygons for the board and stake.

There are only 38 vertices, so the sign costs almost nothing even when dozens line a perimeter. StemCell certification gives this tiny asset several native formats prepared from one master scene. The rough board and plain stake suggest a hasty marker left by soldiers in the field.

Since 2026 the sign has been priced at $24 and suits war games, documentaries and survival scenes. Plant a row along a fence line, or set one alone at the edge of a misty field. Demining charities illustrating the danger of leftover munitions can show this marker in realistic terrain. Its extreme simplicity makes it ideal for mobile games and open worlds where draw distance matters.

A set of worn shipping boxes with open and bent flaps, the cardboard clutter of warehouses, garages and moving days. The Worn Shipping Boxes with Flaps Used Set packs 32,386 polygons into scuffed edges, creases and loose flaps.

Its 32,377 vertices nearly equal the face count, the profile of tidy closed shells despite the wear. StemCell delivery hands you the boxes in many native formats built from one carefully checked scene. Varied flap positions keep the pile from looking repeated, even when several boxes share a shot.

The set entered the catalog in 2026 at $99 and suits storage rooms, logistics scenes and apartment move-ins. Stack them in a garage corner, or scatter a few open boxes across an empty living room floor. Removal companies can illustrate packing advice with boxes that look genuinely used rather than fresh from the store. Open flaps reveal empty interiors, ready for you to fill with books, dishes or wrapped items.

A classroom chalkboard covered in handwritten notes, complete with chalk sticks and a felt eraser on the ledge. The Written Chalkboard with Chalk and Eraser uses 18,928 polygons for the frame, chalk tray and accessories.

There are 19,520 vertices, keeping the chalk cylinders round and the eraser block softly beveled. Its CheckMate status ensures tidy geometry and real classroom proportions on import. Writing already fills the board, so the scene reads as a lesson in progress rather than an empty room.

For $39 the 2026 chalkboard suits school scenes, lecture halls and educational video backdrops. Mount it behind a teacher's desk, or lean it on an easel in a cafe as a menu board. Tutors recording lessons can replace the writing with their own text by editing the board texture. A stub of chalk left in the tray hints at a busy day of teaching and adds subtle realism.

A concrete defense bunker from the Second World War with a rusty gun in its firing slit, built for coastal and battlefield scenes. The WW II Defense Bunker with Rusty Gun Simplified uses 299,517 polygons for the weathered concrete shell and the corroded weapon.

Its 298,474 vertices give the thick walls rounded, battered edges that show decades of exposure. The bunker is CheckMate certified, so the structure arrives with clean geometry and believable military scale. A narrow embrasure frames the barrel, showing how defenders covered beaches and roads from protected positions.

The bunker costs $59 as a 2026 release and suits war games, history documentaries and coastal ruin scenes. Set it into a dune above a beach, or half-bury it in a forest overgrown with moss. Simplified modeling keeps it suitable for open-world games where several fortifications appear at once. History teachers covering the Atlantic Wall can use it to show what soldiers saw from inside.

A beige military pickup carrying the X-MADIS counter-drone system, with sensors and a turret mounted over the bed. The X MADIS Anti Drone Pickup Beige Simplified uses 500,250 polygons for the vehicle body, radar arrays and weapon station.

Its 558,322 vertices keep the sensor domes and wheel arches clean even in close inspection shots. Prepared under CheckMate rules, the vehicle arrives organized at true scale, ready for convoy scenes. The desert beige paint fits arid terrain and marks the truck as a mobile air defense asset.

Introduced in 2026, the vehicle costs $149 and suits military simulations, defense analysis and documentary visuals. Park it at a forward base perimeter, or follow it along a desert road scanning the sky for threats. Defense educators can show how mobile systems protect troops from small drones without classified imagery. A simplified build keeps it practical for wide scenes with several vehicles moving together in formation.

A set of wall-mounted X-ray lightboxes with films clipped in place, the viewing panels found in clinics and radiology rooms. The X Ray Lightbox Set uses 26,404 polygons for the frames, light panels, clips and film sheets.

There are 26,647 vertices, keeping the clip springs and panel bezels sharp in medium shots. CheckMate quality control ensures clean geometry and true wall-mount dimensions for a clinic interior. Backlit films glow against dark rooms, the classic image of a doctor studying a fracture.

At $29 as a 2026 model, the set suits hospital interiors, medical dramas and orthopedic education. Hang the panels behind a consultation desk, or line several along a corridor in an emergency department. Medical schools can swap the films for their own scans to teach image reading in context. Turning on the panel light in your renderer creates instant atmosphere in a dim exam room.
